sections.history: Banashankari is a living temple at Cholachagudda, about 5 km from Badami, in the old Tilakaranya forest; her name joins vana, forest, with Shankari, the consort of Shiva. Popular belief credits the Badami Chalukyas of the seventh century with the original shrine, and some historians think the site older still, with one suggesting an earlier temple of Rashtrakuta times. The building seen today dates from the eighteenth century, raised, according to the historian Sheelkant Pattar, in 1750 by the Maratha chieftain Parashuram Agale. The goddess is revered as a family deity by many households across Karnataka, and the temple has drawn pilgrims for centuries.
sections.architecture: In the sanctum stands a black stone image of the goddess, eight-armed and fierce, seated on a lion and trampling a demon underfoot. Beside the temple lies its great tank, known as Haridra Tirtha or Harishchandra Tirtha, a stone-walled square of some 360 feet a side, with pillared mantapas on three sides. A pillared cloister is built around the water, so that the tank and the temple form a single walled world. The mix of temple, cloister and tank is typical of the Chalukya country’s sacred landscape, where shrine and water are never far apart.
sections.legends: The Skanda Purana and the Padma Purana tell of the demon Durgamasura, who tormented the region until the gods begged for help. The goddess came to earth as Shakambari and, after a fierce battle, slew him. Her name carries a second story: when famine gripped the world, she is said to have nourished the starving with green vegetables and fruit from her own being, which is why Shakambari means the one who bears greens. The forest setting in which she is worshipped, Tilakaranya, gives her the name Banashankari, the goddess of the forest.
sections.festivals: The Banashankari Jatre is the great festival, beginning on the full moon of the Kannada month of Pushya, in January or February, and lasting ten to twelve days, with the temple car procession, the rathotsava, as its centrepiece. During Navaratri the goddess is adorned in different ornaments and sarees for nine days. Crowds are largest at these times; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Arrive in the morning, when the courtyard is busy with families bringing offerings of coconuts and flowers. After darshan, walk the cloister around the tank and watch its stone steps catch the light. On festival days the lanes of Cholachagudda fill with devotees and traders, while on ordinary days the temple is calm. It makes a fitting living counterpart to the ancient stone monuments of Badami, Mahakuta and Pattadakal.

visit.timings: A living temple with daily worship, with hours that are longer around the Jatre and Navaratri. Confirm timings locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is usually restricted inside the sanctum; ask at the temple before taking photographs of the deity or of worshippers.
visit.gettingThere: Cholachagudda is in Bagalkot district, about 5 km from Badami by road; autos and taxis from Badami cover the short drive. Badami has the nearest railway station, and the nearest airport is Hubballi.
